legend: Technical artefact due to poorly cleaned slides. During the transport of the glass slides from manufacturer to bedside, small glass particles are released. During the smearing process, these particles and dust are dragged with the FNAB material, causing these gaps in the smear.

Technical artefact due to fibrin clot formation in contaminating blood, forming in the needle due to too long a period of the needle being in the lesion and once withdrawn from the target lesion. Cells are caught up in the fibrin, making them difficult to evaluate.
Technical artefact due to fragile lymphocytes caught up in fibrin strands and then overly forcibly smeared, to form strings of chromatinic smearing.
Technical artefact due to ultrasound gel left on the skin, the probe, or the plastic covering the probe. The gel is more obscuring in Giemsa than Pap stains, and it distorts any cells present.
Lymph node direct smears usually display stripped nuclei and cytoplasmic debris, which hamper immune assessment, in particular when dealing with a group of differentiation antibodies (Giemsa).

Lymph node cytospins provide excellent material not only for cytomorphological evaluation, but also for immunocytochemistry. The absorption of the liquid that soaks the cells, which is rich in immunoreactive debris, during the cytospins procedure provides clean immunostain with good staining and no background (Pap).

Lymph node cell blocks are better prepared from high-cellularity fluids, with the advantage that numerous sections can be prepared. They provide well-preserved cytomorphology and tissue architecture. Immunostains can be easily applied, using validated techniques for immunocytochemistry of histopathology specimens (haematoxylin).

legend: Direct smear from FNAB in cyclin D1 immunocytochemistry, showing contaminating background (immunocytochemistry).
Cytospin preparation undergoing cyclin D1 immunocytochemistry showing clean background.
Cell block showing diagnostic positive staining for cyclin D1 in immunocytochemistry.

The FNAB material can be placed in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), RPMI medium, or buffered saline for flow cytometry; directly placed, smeared, and air-dried for ROSE using a Giemsa stain and smeared and immediately placed in 100% alcohol for Pap stain; or placed in PBS, RPMI medium, buffered saline, or buffered formalin for cell block preparation.
